newsitem.title: UK: S.Korean metal probe not a concern yet - LME trader.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean metal probe not a concern yet - LME trader.

text.p: News that South Korea's Finance Ministry was investigating overseas futures trading by Korean companies caused little immediate concern to London Metal Exchange (LME) traders.
Korean brokers and traders said on Monday the ministry was probing a recent sharp increase in South Korean base metal futures and options trading on the LME.
"It's interesting to see how this develops, but news of an investigation is not going to move the market," an LME floor trader said.
During this year, rumours have flared up at times over trading operations by one particular South Korean firm. There are four major brokerage companies that transact LME business.
Some said that problems could arise if a company were granting forward options to secure premium income with a view to using this to meet immediate margin requirements.
However, this is difficult to ascertain, and would only be borne out in coming months if the market were to move to levels where those options became exercisible.
"The only way this would have an impact is if one of the companies were to default or if they were stopped from trading. Then volumes would fall," another trader said.
The South Korean ministry official summoned several domestic brokers Monday, following a relaxation in April of several regulations regarding overseas futures trading.
Korea's government has eased the open position limit for domestic futures traders to allow open positions exceeding traders yearly physical volume.
Some traders here said that it would be difficult to keep volumes and open interest in futures and options equal to physical volume because of the need to keep fine-tuning hedge strategies.
"To hedge properly, there is every reason for someone to be trading in excess of physical volume," one said.
South Korea's futures and options volumes surged to 485,558 lots in the first four months of 1997, against 43,293 lots in the same 1996 period. Turnover for the whole of 1996 was 503,553 lots.

Korean traders said that LG Metals Corp, South Korea's largest copper producer and an affiliate of LG Group, was believed to be largely responsible for the recent rise in South Korea's metal futures/options turnover.

Earlier this month a company spokesman said the metals market had no need to worry about its current open LME metal options positions, but he declined to comment on rumours in London the firm was facing huge losses after a rally in copper.

In London, regulatory and market authorities had a low-key response to the investigation. The LME was not available for comment, while Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO) said it had not been approached by the Koreans.
